newsitem.title: USA: Mass. would expand bottle bill to all drinks.
newsitem.headline: Mass. would expand bottle bill to all drinks.

text.p: A majority the Massachusetts Legislature has signed on to a bill that would expand the $0.05 deposit currently applied to containers of carbonated drinks and beers to all beverages, proponents said Wednesday.

At a Beacon Hill press conference, legislators announced their support for the measure that would add sports drinks, bottled water, wine and fruit juices in bottles or cans to a 14-year-old law that already requires shopkeepers to collect an extra nickel deposit on cans and bottles of carbonated soda and malt beverages.

Since passed in 1982, between 80 percent and 85 percent of beer and soda containers are returned and recycled every year, said Amy Perry, a spokeswoman for MASSPIRG, a consumer interest group. She estimated some two billion containers were recycled annually. Expanding the coverage would boost that to four billion containers annually, she said.

On those containers that are not returned, Massachusetts collects about $12 million to $15 million annually. The money is supposed to go to a trust fund designed to support recycling projects. In the past, the money has been used for other environmental needs, such as hazardous waste disposal.

"In the 14 years since the bottle bill became law...recycling has become a way of life in Massachusetts," said Sen. Lois Pines, who co-authored the original legislation and hoped the expanded legislation "would take in a new generation of drinks."

Sen. Warren Tollman, noting that 21 of the state's 40 senators and 90 of the state's 160 House members had co-signed the measure, said it stands a good chance of "getting out of committee this year." The measure has been introduced for the past five sessions, but has failed to make it to the floor in either house.
Pines said she expected the measure's opponents, bottling companies and beverage firms, would make a concerted effort to defeat the measure. "But we've seen this before. This is not a major change."

Ron Bottrell, a spokesman for Quaker Oats Co, which makes Snapple and Gatorade drinks, declined to comment on the measure. Spokesmen for Coca-Cola Co and PepsiCo Inc, whose companies make non-carbonated juices and teas as well as soft drinks, did not return phone calls. And the Grocery Manufacturers Association could not be reached for comment.

The International Bottled Water Association, in a statement, said of the measure, "Forced deposit systems for beverage containers increase the cost for manufacturers, distributors and ultimately the consumer.
"Our association will continue to oppose any legislation that would expand the current forced deposit system to include additional beverages, including bottled water."
